summary: This feature article, part of a series on aging and geriatric health, explains why regular health screenings matter for older adults, drawing on interviews with a physician, gerontologist, nurse practitioner, public health expert and digital health technologist. It covers early detection, mental health and social benefits, barriers such as accessibility and patient resistance, policy and Medicare efforts, digital tools, and local community outreach programs.
one_line: Interviews with five experts and community examples show how regular health screenings help the elderly and how barriers to them can be overcome.
key_facts: Dr. Susan Hartman, with over two decades in geriatric healthcare, was interviewed on September 15, 2023 and said screenings provide a baseline to identify health changes, often before symptoms appear.
Hartman says conditions like hypertension, diabetes, and cancer can be silent for years, and early detection can significantly alter the disease trajectory.
Hartman notes that loneliness can be as detrimental to health as smoking fifteen cigarettes a day according to some studies, and screening visits' social interaction helps counteract it.
Gerontologist Dr. Alex Greene, interviewed on October 5, 2023, named accessibility as a biggest challenge, citing mobility issues and areas with limited healthcare facilities.
Dr. Greene also cites patient resistance, stemming from fear, misinformation, or a belief that health issues are an inevitable part of aging.
Dr. Greene points to mobile clinics and telemedicine as creative solutions to bring healthcare professionals to those who need it most.
Nurse Practitioner Emily Torres, interviewed on November 10, 2023, says screenings reveal issues patients were unaware of, such as depression or early signs of cognitive impairment.
Torres describes screenings as touchpoints for social determinants of health like food insecurity and social isolation.
Public health expert Mark Richardson, interviewed on December 2, 2023, works with insurance companies and the government to make screenings more accessible and affordable.
Richardson says Medicare coverage for annual wellness visits is a step in the right direction but awareness needs raising and access needs simplifying.
Richardson's programs include health fairs and workshops tailored to seniors, in partnership with local organizations, to make screenings less intimidating.

Dr. Lisa Chang, a digital health technologist interviewed on January 15, 2024, cites electronic medical records and wearable devices that monitor vital signs in real time, while warning of the digital divide among the elderly.
Local initiatives include a church health ministry offering blood pressure checks every Sunday and a community center's monthly diabetes education sessions.
